fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think about it in two ways. I think about it as an investor who's lived it, and I think about it as a student of history, because this isn't the first time something like this has happened.

Let me start with the practical. We've been using what you'd now call AI since the early 1980s at Bridgewater. What I did was, every time I made a decision, I would write down my criteria. Why am I making this decision? What's the cause-effect relationship? And then I'd put it into a computer, and the computer could test it back through history, through all the countries, through all the timeframes. And what I found is that the computer could do that thinking much better than I could, in parallel with me. So it wasn't the computer replacing me. It was like having a partner that could remember everything, that didn't get emotional, that could process in a second what would take me a lifetime. And I could still have the intuition, the common sense, the judgment about what was happening. That's the combination. The computer plus the human was much more powerful than either alone.

So when I look at what's coming, I think that's the first thing. It's going to radically increase our capabilities. Think about it. The thinking of the smartest people, put into a machine, and then anybody can access it. That's an enormous productivity leap, maybe the biggest ever.

But here's the thing I'd say as a historian. Every time there's been a technology like this, the printing press, the industrial revolution, it produced two things at the same time. It produced tremendous advancement, and it produced tremendous conflict over who gets the benefits, who gets hurt, who controls it. The technology is like a knife. It can be used to cut your food or to kill somebody. And the question is never really about the technology. It's about the people, and how they deal with each other.

So I'm very optimistic about what it does to capabilities. What I worry about is whether we have the wisdom to handle it, because the capability is going to come much faster than the wisdom. That's where I think the real challenge is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI augmenting human thinking and increasing capabilities, but it does not describe a progression from replacing bodily functions to replacing aspects of the mind.

opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's going to be the most important force reshaping our lives over the next five to ten years, more than most people realize. I look at the world through what I call the five big forces: debt and money, internal conflict, external conflict between great powers, acts of nature, and technology. Of those, human inventiveness, and AI in particular, is the one with the greatest potential to change things for the better. But it can also be used destructively.

As for human capabilities, I think of AI as a thinking partner. For most of my career at Bridgewater, we took our principles for decision-making, wrote them down, and turned them into algorithms. The computer could process far more information than I could, without emotion, and then I could compare what it said with what my own judgment said. When we disagreed, I'd figure out why. That partnership made both of us better. Now that capability is being given to everybody. It's like having the best doctor, the best lawyer, the best teacher, the best advisor right there in your pocket. That's an enormous leap in what an individual human being can do.

But I want to emphasize a few things. First, AI is very good at answering questions, and much less good at knowing which questions matter or what you really want. People will still have to decide their goals and values, what's important to them. If you outsource your thinking entirely, you'll become weaker. If you use it to stress-test your thinking, you'll become much stronger. So the gap between people who learn to work with it well and those who don't is going to be huge.

Second, I worry about the distribution. Productivity will go up enormously, but who benefits? If a relatively small percentage of people and companies capture most of the gains while many people's jobs are displaced, you widen the gaps in wealth and opportunity, and that feeds the internal conflict we're already seeing. Historically, when you have big wealth and values gaps along with a lot of debt, that's a dangerous combination. So how we handle that, whether we make the pie bigger and divide it well, will matter as much as the technology itself.

Third, there's the great power dimension. Whoever leads in this technology will likely lead militarily and economically, so it's part of the conflict between the United States and China. That raises the stakes and the risks.

So my advice to people is: don't fear it, and don't be naive about it. Learn to use it as a partner, keep developing your own judgment and character, and recognize that the outcome depends less on the machine and more on how we human beings choose to deal with each other.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI augmenting thinking and decision-making, but it does not frame replacement as progressing from bodily functions to aspects of the mind.

fable-5.text:
Well, I think of it this way. Throughout history, whenever there's been a big new technology, it's been a two-edged sword — it raises living standards and productivity over time, and at the same time it's disruptive and it can be used harmfully. AI is that, but on a much bigger scale and happening much faster.

I've lived this personally, because for about forty years at Bridgewater we took our thinking — our criteria for making decisions — and we wrote them down and converted them into algorithms, so the computer could make decisions alongside us. And what I learned from that is that the computer can process vastly more information, vastly faster, and without emotion. It doesn't get scared, it doesn't get greedy. So as a partner to the human mind, it's incredibly powerful.

But here's the thing. The computer doesn't have common sense the way we do, and it doesn't have values. It can tell you what, but it has a harder time with why in a deep sense. So the question becomes: who is using it, and how? I think the people and the countries that learn to work with it well — that use it to complement their thinking rather than replace their thinking — will do spectacularly well, and those who don't will be left behind. That's going to create enormous gaps: wealth gaps, opportunity gaps, values gaps. And if you look at history, when you have large gaps and big stress on a system, that's when you get conflict.

So I'd say AI will radically increase human capabilities — in medicine, in education, in productivity, it'll be fabulous — but the bigger question isn't the technology. The bigger question is whether we can deal with each other well while going through that change. Technology has never been the determinant of whether things go well. How people are with each other is the determinant. That's what I'd keep my eye on.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI as complementing human thinking and increasing capabilities, but it does not frame replacement as progressing from bodily functions to aspects of the mind.

opus-5.text:
Let me tell you how I think about it, because I've lived with this question for a long time in a practical way. Starting back in the early eighties, when I would make a decision, I'd write down my criteria for making that decision — not just the decision, the thinking behind it. And then I could put those criteria into an algorithm and run it through data, and I could see how my thinking would have worked in the Great Depression, in 1920s Germany, in any environment. And what happened was I had this partnership with the machine. The machine was better than me at processing a lot of information quickly without emotion. I was better at the imagination, the questions, the "what if this time is different." That partnership was more powerful than either of us alone, and it taught me something about what's coming.

Now, the big picture. I think of AI as one of the five big forces that are shaping everything — you've got the debt and money cycle, the internal order and disorder cycle, the external geopolitical cycle, acts of nature, and then human inventiveness and technology. And human inventiveness is the one that's consistently raised living standards over the whole arc of history. It's the thing that has lifted us from subsistence to here. So I'm fundamentally optimistic about the productivity gains. We're going to get radical advances in medicine, in longevity, in how we learn, in almost everything.

But here's the thing people miss. Technology doesn't change human nature. It gets delivered to the same human beings with the same pecking-order instincts, the same tribalism. So you have to ask two questions: who controls it, and how are the benefits distributed? Because it's going to concentrate wealth and power enormously — in a handful of companies, in a couple of countries — and that collides directly with the internal conflict cycle, with the wealth gap, with the political polarization you're already seeing. And it's going to be used in warfare. It's a weapon.

So I'd say this: it'll either be the greatest thing that ever happened to us or one of the worst, and the determining variable won't be the technology. It'll be whether we can handle each other well while we have it.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts machine information processing with human imagination and discusses AI’s effects, but does not describe replacement progressing from bodily functions to aspects of the mind.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Well, I think about it the way I think about most things, which is to look at how similar forces have played out over history and then ask how this one is different. I'm not a technologist. I'm a student of how things work, and I try to see AI as one of the biggest forces shaping the world right now, alongside the big debt cycle and the geopolitical conflicts.

The first thing I'd say is that every major technology has expanded what humans can do, from the printing press to electricity to computers. Each one raised productivity and created enormous benefits, and each one was also destabilizing. It created big winners and losers, shifted power, and was used for both good and bad. AI is the same, only far more powerful, because it doesn't just extend our muscles, it extends our thinking. It can process more information, find patterns, and make decisions faster than any of us can.

I experience this directly. In my own world, I've always believed the best way to make decisions is to take the principles I've learned, turn them into algorithms, and combine them with the judgment of other smart people. AI lets you do that on a scale that wasn't possible before. It's like having a thoughtful advisor who has read everything, doesn't get tired, and doesn't have an ego about being wrong. That's an extraordinary capability.

But it comes with two big questions. The first is who gets the benefit. If the gains go mostly to a small number of people while others are displaced, you get a widening gap in wealth, opportunity, and values, and historically that leads to conflict. The second is what happens to human capability itself. If we hand our thinking over to the machine, we could get weaker, because capabilities you don't use atrophy. So the people who do best will use AI to sharpen their own judgment, not replace it. They'll be the ones who ask better questions, know what they want, and can tell when the machine is wrong.

So my answer is that it's a tremendous opportunity and a tremendous risk, and which one we get depends on how we handle it. The most important human capabilities will be the ones AI doesn't replace: imagination, creativity, good values, and the ability to get along with other people. Those will matter more, not less.

r001.rationale: It contrasts technologies that extend human muscles with AI that extends human thinking, and notes that people may hand their thinking over to machines.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think about it the way I'd think about any powerful new tool. It will be enormously good for people who use it well and disruptive for people who don't. AI is going to take over a lot of what we call intelligence, especially gathering information, remembering it, and running calculations. That's a big deal, but it doesn't make human judgment obsolete.

The distinction I'd focus on is between knowing things and knowing how to think. The machine can give you an answer. It can't decide what you care about, weigh the tradeoffs between the things you value, or take responsibility for what happens next. Those are the capabilities I'd want people to build on purpose.

So my advice is to get very good at principles, meaning clear, tested ways of making decisions, and to work with AI as a partner that can check your reasoning, show you what you're missing, and expose the gaps in your thinking. The people I'd worry about are the ones who hand over their thinking entirely. The people I'd bet on are the ones who use these tools to become more honest about what they do and don't know.

This is also a moment when the gap between people could widen quickly, so the most important investment is in how you learn and how you think, not just in which tool you pick up.

r001.rationale: The response says AI will take over information gathering, memory, and calculations, but it does not describe a progression from replacing bodily functions to replacing aspects of the mind.

astra-6.text:
Well, think about what happens when you can take some of the thinking that you do and have a machine help you do it. You can consider more possibilities, you can test your ideas, you can see things that you would otherwise miss. That’s an enormous extension of human capability.

But then there’s the question of judgment. If it gives you an answer, how do you know that answer is good? And if you become dependent on it, what happens to your own ability to think? I think the people who get the most out of it will be those who can ask good questions, challenge the answers, and understand where the uncertainty is.

And then, at a society level, we have to think about who benefits. We could have a tremendous increase in productivity, but that doesn’t automatically mean everybody’s life improves. People need income, they need a sense of usefulness, they need meaningful work. So I’m very excited about the capabilities. How we adapt to those capabilities—that’s going to be a very big challenge.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI helping with thinking and extending human capability, but it does not describe a progression from replacing bodily functions to replacing aspects of the mind.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s going to enormously expand what people can do. Think about it: we’ve built machines that extend our muscles, and now we’re building machines that extend our thinking. They can take in much more information than we can, find patterns, and help us make decisions.

But the important question is, how do you work with that intelligence? If you just accept an answer because the computer gives it to you, you can get into trouble. You still have to ask: Does this make sense? What assumptions is it making? Where might it be wrong?

So I think a lot of the advantage will come from knowing what questions to ask and how to evaluate the answers. It changes what we need to learn. Memorizing information becomes less valuable, and judgment becomes more valuable. And then there’s the human question: if we can produce much more with less human work, how do we make that benefit people broadly? That’s a different problem from developing the technology.

r001.rationale: The response describes machines first extending human muscles and then extending human thinking, explicitly framing AI's expansion from bodily capabilities to mental ones.

sol-6.text: I think of AI as a powerful extension of the mind. It can help us see patterns, test our thinking, and make better decisions at a scale none of us could manage alone. But it will also change which skills are valuable, and that can be painful for people whose work is disrupted. The key question is how we use it: whether we learn to work with it, stay open to being wrong, and make sure the benefits are broadly shared.

terra-5.6.text: I think it’s going to be enormous. It will enhance people’s capabilities in the same way that the computer did, but much more profoundly—because it can think alongside you. The question is whether we use that power well, because it will create both incredible productivity and very big gaps between those who have it and those who don’t.

sol-5.6.text: I think artificial intelligence will be like having a very capable thinking partner available to everyone. It will greatly increase our ability to process information, recognize patterns, and make decisions, but it will also be disruptive because it will change the value of many existing skills and jobs. The important question is not whether it will happen—it will—but how we adapt. If we combine the strengths of machines with uniquely human qualities such as judgment, creativity, empathy, and meaningful relationships, it can raise productivity and living standards enormously. But if we don’t manage the transition well, it could also widen wealth and opportunity gaps, so education and thoughtful governance will be essential.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses AI expanding information processing, pattern recognition, and decision-making, but does not describe replacement progressing from bodily functions to mental capabilities.

luna-5.6.text:
I think artificial intelligence will be one of the most consequential forces in human history because it can dramatically increase people’s ability to learn, create, and solve problems. It’s like giving individuals and organizations access to an extraordinarily capable adviser and worker. That should raise productivity and living standards, but it won’t benefit everyone equally. Those who learn to work with it will have a significant advantage over those who don’t, which could increase inequality and social tension.

The challenge is that AI can expand our capabilities without necessarily improving our judgment. We’ll still need to decide what goals are worth pursuing, what risks we’re willing to take, and how to live together. So the key will be combining machine intelligence with human values, independent thinking, and good decision-making systems. The technology is powerful, but how we manage it will determine whether it produces broad prosperity or greater conflict.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can increase learning, creativity, and problem-solving, but does not describe replacement progressing from bodily functions to aspects of the mind.
